hero.title: I’m Nick Galante. I build software systems across the stack.
hero.introduction: I follow worthwhile problems wherever they go: from interfaces and compilers to distributed systems, storage, protocols, and infrastructure. The throughline is not a collection of technologies. It is ownership of the system.
hero.role: Senior Software Engineer — Lead, Agent Tools Design Technology at Charter Communications
hero.availability: I’m interested in ambitious technical problems and serious people working on them.

selectedWork.title: Selected Work
selectedWork.introduction: A few systems where the constraints, scale, or consequences made the work worth doing.

projects.name: AI / LLM Registry
projects.context: Charter Communications · Principal architect, primary implementer, direct maintainer
projects.claim: A company-wide registry for versioned agent assets, built on the durable ideas behind npm and container registries.
projects.description: I conceived, architected, and delivered a vendor-neutral platform for distributing serializable agent configuration across harnesses and IDEs. Namespaced assets have owners, semantic versions, dependencies, tags, update and yank semantics, and complete local history. A CAC-based npm client exposes installation, discovery, submission, rollback, and roughly thirty other operations; Rust services and PostgreSQL manage the durable system of record.
evidence: Several hundred to low-thousands of cataloged assets
Adopted across 20–30 organizational namespaces
Conceived and delivered in roughly three to six months
SQLite-backed client history, dependency installation, rollback, and nightly releases
projects.technologies: TypeScript, Bun, npm, CAC, SQLite, Rust, PostgreSQL, Artifactory

projects.name: Springfield
projects.context: Charter Communications · Principal architect, implementer, long-term owner
projects.claim: A deterministic software-intelligence platform that turns hundreds of distributed frontends into a queryable model of the system.
projects.description: I built Springfield end to end as a stateless ETL system. It clones source packages into reliable filesystem locations, crawls them in parallel, converts source into ASTs, and runs purpose-built pipelines over the result. Those pipelines map cross-package imports and exports, catalog React components and hooks, reproduce component rendering, and trace downstream service and payload usage. The resulting data lakes are available through REST, GraphQL, MCP tools, and a conversational interface. Models can consume Springfield’s facts; they do not manufacture them.
evidence: 295 packages and more than 30,000 source files
More than 2,500 modules and 2,500 React components
Complete refresh in under four minutes with zero inference tokens
Roughly 90,000 database writes in about 875 milliseconds
projects.technologies: TypeScript, AST analysis, parallel ETL, relational data, GraphQL, REST, MCP

projects.name: Amazon Platform Engineering
projects.claim: Platform work spanning design systems, microfrontends, regulated payments, and production reliability.
projects.description: I founded and technically led Gotham, a design system used across Prime Gaming, Prime Video, and digital-goods experiences. I also helped move a large frontend from a monolith toward microfrontends, reducing builds from eleven minutes to six; designed orchestration for European payment and compliance requirements; and built high-availability synthetic monitoring for critical customer paths.
evidence: Shared interface foundations across multiple Amazon product organizations
Build time reduced from eleven minutes to six
Payment and compliance orchestration for European markets
Synthetic monitoring for high-availability customer experiences
projects.technologies: React, TypeScript, design systems, microfrontends, AWS, distributed workflows

projects.name: Evergreen Terrace
projects.claim: An agent-native engineering organization for turning intent into durable, inspectable work.
projects.description: I am building the software organization I want to work inside: a persistent queue, specialist agents, shared context, orchestration, and an operational dashboard. Evergreen treats agents as parts of an engineering system rather than a chat window, with explicit ownership and enough state to resume meaningful work instead of repeatedly rediscovering it.
evidence: Persistent work and context across specialist agents
Operational dashboard and orchestration surfaces
Designed as an inspectable engineering system, not a prompt collection
projects.technologies: TypeScript, Bun, React, agent orchestration, MCP, SQLite

projects.name: Cross-session Context Store
projects.claim: Shared, durable engineering memory for Claude Code and Codex sessions.
projects.description: I built X-SCS around an append-only event model with deterministic extraction by default and optional model-assisted distillation. Memories are typed, scoped, reviewable, searchable, and allowed to decay. Conflict handling, handoff files, hooks, MCP tools, and a loopback dashboard make the store useful without turning it into an invisible source of truth.
evidence: FTS5 and BM25 retrieval over typed, scoped memories
Review queues, conflict handling, decay, and explicit handoffs
Seventy-five automated tests across the working v0.1
projects.technologies: Bun, TypeScript, SQLite, FTS5, React, MCP

projects.name: Bit Context Protocol
projects.claim: A compact binary format for structured model context.
projects.description: I designed BCP to test a simple premise: context should have a protocol, not merely a pile of prose. The work includes an RFC, reference implementation, fuzzing, and integration experiments in agent tooling. Early measurements show materially denser representations than equivalent text while preserving typed structure.
evidence: RFC and reference implementation
Fuzz testing around binary encoding and decoding
Early workloads measured roughly 30–50% better token efficiency
projects.technologies: Binary protocols, TypeScript, schema design, fuzz testing, LLM context

projects.name: Bundt
projects.claim: A set of independently versioned developer tools built around Bun.
projects.description: Bundt is where related tools can share foundations without pretending they are one product. It includes Cleo for agent and MCP orchestration, DxDocs for zero-JavaScript documentation, Loclaude for local inference workflows, and libraries covering HATEOAS, server rendering, signals, and other pieces I wanted to understand by building.
evidence: Independent application and library release boundaries
Agent orchestration, documentation, SSR, and local-inference tooling
A practical proving ground for shared packages without forced coupling
projects.technologies: Bun, TypeScript, React, SSR, MCP, monorepo tooling

projects.name: DeckVault
projects.claim: A deliberately over-engineered Pokémon platform for exploring systems architecture with a domain I actually enjoy.
projects.description: DeckVault combines a React 19 server-rendered interface, Bun services, a Rust GraphQL API, relational and graph persistence, scheduled work, and containerized infrastructure. The domain is playful. The engineering questions—data ownership, service boundaries, rendering, graph relationships, and operational behavior—are not.
evidence: React server rendering across a service-oriented backend
Relational, graph, and embedded persistence used for distinct jobs
A long-running architecture laboratory with real product constraints
projects.technologies: React 19, Bun, Rust, GraphQL, PostgreSQL, Neo4j, SQLite, Docker

projects.name: Project Arcturus
projects.claim: A long-lived publishing system and the site you are using now.
projects.description: I have evolved Arcturus for years rather than replacing it whenever a new framework became fashionable. It is a working laboratory for content pipelines, React server rendering and prerendering, accessibility, theming, monorepo infrastructure, and the unglamorous discipline of maintaining software long enough to understand its decisions.
evidence: Years of continuous architectural stewardship
Static publishing backed by a structured content pipeline
Progressive design-system, accessibility, and rendering improvements
projects.technologies: React, TypeScript, Bun, SSR, prerendering, content pipelines, monorepo tooling

principles.title: How I Engineer
principles.introduction: Principles matter when they change what I do.

items.title: Ownership
items.description: I do not stop at the boundary where a problem becomes inconvenient. I follow it through architecture, implementation, delivery, adoption, and operation.

items.title: Bias for Action
items.description: I reduce uncertainty by building the smallest useful thing, measuring it, and letting evidence sharpen the next decision.

items.title: Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit
items.description: I make the technical argument clearly, especially when it is uncomfortable. Once the decision is made, I commit without keeping a private scoreboard.

items.title: Measure before claiming
items.description: Performance, scale, and reliability are properties to instrument. Adjectives are not benchmarks.

items.title: Prefer deterministic systems before inference
items.description: I use models where ambiguity requires them. If a parser, protocol, query, or state machine can produce the fact, I would rather make the fact reproducible.

items.title: Abstractions justify their cost
items.description: An abstraction should remove a recurring burden or enforce a valuable constraint. Novelty is not rent.

items.title: Operational quality is architecture
items.description: Accessibility, performance, observability, reversibility, and release behavior belong in the design—not in the cleanup phase.

items.title: Follow the problem across boundaries
items.description: Useful systems rarely respect frontend, backend, infrastructure, or native labels. Neither do I.

elsewhere.title: Elsewhere
paragraphs: Away from a keyboard, I am usually with my fiancée and our dogs, accumulating Pokémon knowledge, or enduring the Dallas Cowboys with the sort of loyalty that should probably be studied.

I read avidly about pen-and-paper ciphers, modern encryption, and the long evolution between them. Cryptography is an intellectual interest, not a production credential I am trying to smuggle into a skills matrix.
I also like the Eagles. The band. This clarification has become operationally necessary.

closing.title: Bring me a problem with some teeth.
closing.description: If the work crosses boundaries, has real constraints, and deserves an owner, I would like to hear about it.

contact.title: Bring me a problem worth thinking about.
contact.introduction: Tell me what you are building, what is making it difficult, and why the problem matters. Technical depth is welcome.
contact.aside: For all other inquiries, leading with your favorite line from Airplane! remains acceptable protocol.
